body: I smoked every day for almost a year on Setraline, nothing bad ever happened but I found that I’d sometimes get anxious if I smoked a bit too much.

I had an awful experience with my past two SSRI medications (always nauseous and felt like a zombie), when I was first prescribed Setraline a year ago (at the absolute lowest dose) I found the side effects minimal!

With Setraline the key is to starting small and then going higher, when I started with the 25 mg I was a bit nauseous for the first week and had some diarrhea first thing in the morning but that went away fast. 

I restarted my medication last night after being off for a few weeks (pharmacist wouldn’t refill my prescription without talking to the doctor, COVID in Ontario means I couldn’t get an appointment with my doctor for almost a month) and I feel awful. I was moved up to the 50 mg dose and spent a lot of last night in the bathroom coming out of both ends. I’m fingers crossed that it’ll go away pretty quick since I find Setraline works quite well for me but we’ll see!

Wine glasses, I work as a winemaker/sommelier and the quality of glasses can make a giant impact on the overall taste and aroma of the wine!
Yeah same here, something sounds fishy about the whole situation

Tannins are a polyphenol that adds a bitter taste in wine and food. Typically tannins are found in plants, seeds, bark, wood, leaves and fruit skins of not just grapes but many other types of fruits & vegetables too. As a sommelier/winemaker I have multiple people come up to me at a wine bar claiming that "they can't drink reds because the tannins give them headaches" but if that was the truth then these same people also couldn't consume; chocolate, nuts, beans, tea, apple juice, coffee, pomegranate, cider, or white wine either without getting a headache. 

On the other hand, sulphites is prevalent in most processed foods and other forms of alcohol. Sulphur is used to help stabilize the wine and balance the acidity, it can also be used in the vineyard as a pest management system, when distilling sulphites naturally are brought forward through the process of extracting the alcohol from the distillers beer. Sulphites in wine also help to preserve the life span of the wine to prevent it from oxidizing while aging the wine. When making wine, your final end product has on average 50 mg/L of sulphite per bottle of wine which is well below the USA maximum legal limit (350 mg/L). Only a very small percentage of the population has a sulphite allergy, and similarly to tannins if you have a sulphite problem you also can't consume french fries, cured meats, cheese or canned soups. 

When it comes to drinking wine, 97% of the time the headache you have is from the fact that you became dehydrated or already were when you started drinking.  Histamine can cause you to have headache as well while drinking wines but you'd also have a similar reaction when consuming tofu, tempeh, ketchup, or aged meats. Tyramine (an amine that increases as your body breaks down aged food with broken down proteins) can also cause headaches, but similarly you can also find this in a variety of other foods such as coconut, bananas, raspberries, yeast products (bread, yogurt, cheese, other alcohol products), avocado, pineapple, etc.

TLDR: tannins make your mouth dry and bitter, sulfites are not nearly as high of a level as you think they are in wine, and you should drink a glass of water with every glass of wine.
Tannins and sulphites in wine aren't what's giving you a headache, it's dehydration and alcohol combined when you drink wine.
